modules.title: Semantic HTML
modules.summary: Markup that describes what things are, not only how they look.

lessons.title: HTML That Means Something
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Elements carry meaning, and meaning is functionality

A `<button>` is focusable, activates on Enter and Space, and announces itself as a button to a screen reader. A `<div onclick>` does none of that, and you must reimplement all of it — usually incompletely.

Using the right element is not a style preference. It is the difference between something that works for everyone and something that works for people using a mouse.

## The structural elements

`<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<article>`, `<section>`, `<aside>`, `<footer>`. Screen reader users navigate by these landmarks, jumping straight to the main content instead of hearing the navigation on every page.

One `<main>` per page, containing the primary content.

## Headings form an outline

`<h1>` through `<h6>` are a document outline, not font sizes. Skipping from `<h1>` to `<h4>` because it looked right breaks navigation for anyone moving through the page by heading.

One `<h1>`, then descend in order, and set the visual size with CSS.

## Lists, tables and figures

Use `<ul>` for a list so assistive technology announces "list, five items". Use `<table>` for tabular data with `<th>` and `scope` so cells are associated with their headers.

A table used for layout is a page that reads as nonsense aloud.

## Images need honest alt text

`alt` describes what the image conveys in context. A decorative image takes `alt=""` so it is skipped — which is correct and deliberate. Omitting `alt` entirely makes a screen reader read the filename.

Do not write "image of"; that is already announced.

## Validate

The W3C validator catches unclosed tags, duplicate ids and nesting errors in seconds. Browsers silently repair a lot of broken markup, so problems stay invisible until something depends on the structure.

lessons.title: Forms, Labels and Input That Works
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Every input needs a label

A `<label>` with a `for` matching the input's `id` does three things: it announces the field to a screen reader, it makes the label text a click target that focuses the input, and it makes the form's purpose readable.

Placeholder text is not a label. It disappears the moment someone types, leaving no indication of what the field was, and its contrast is usually too low to read.

## The input type matters

`type="email"`, `type="tel"`, `type="number"`, `type="date"`. On a phone these change the keyboard that appears — an email field that shows an email keyboard saves real effort.

They also bring free validation and, for dates, a native picker.

## Use the browser's validation, then check on the server

`required`, `minlength`, `pattern` and `type` give immediate feedback with no JavaScript.

None of it is security. Anyone can bypass it entirely. Validate again on the server, always — client validation is a convenience for honest users.

## Autocomplete is an accessibility feature

`autocomplete="email"`, `"name"`, `"street-address"`. It lets the browser fill fields correctly, which matters enormously for anyone who finds typing difficult.

Use the standard token names; a made-up value does nothing.

## Errors must be associated, not just coloured

Colour alone excludes colour-blind users and conveys nothing to a screen reader. Put the error in text, link it with `aria-describedby`, and set `aria-invalid`.

Then the error is announced when the field is focused, rather than being an invisible red border.

## Group related controls

A set of radio buttons belongs in a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`. Without it, each option is announced with no indication of the question being answered.

## Submit buttons say what they do

"Submit" is vague. "Create account" tells the user what is about to happen, which matters most for anyone who cannot see the surrounding context.

modules.title: CSS Layout
modules.summary: The box model and the two layout systems that replaced everything before them.

lessons.title: The Box Model and Why Everything Is Off by a Bit
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Four layers

Every element is content, surrounded by padding, then a border, then margin. Understanding which of those the `width` property refers to explains most layout confusion.

## The default is unhelpful

By default, `width: 300px` sets the **content** width. Add 20px of padding and a 1px border and the element occupies 342px.

So two boxes set to `width: 50%` with any padding overflow their container, and the layout breaks for a reason that is invisible in the CSS.

## `border-box` fixes it

`box-sizing: border-box` makes `width` include padding and border. `width: 300px` means the element is 300px wide, which is what everyone expects.

Apply it to everything, once, at the top of the stylesheet. Every CSS framework does this and so should you.

## Margins collapse vertically

Two stacked elements with 20px bottom and 30px top margins have 30px between them, not 50px. Only the larger applies.

This surprises people, and it only happens vertically, and only outside flex and grid containers — which is one more reason modern layout is less confusing than what came before.

## `display` decides the rules

`block` takes full width and stacks. `inline` flows in text and ignores width and vertical margins. `inline-block` flows but accepts dimensions. `flex` and `grid` make the element a layout container for its children.

Trying to set the height of an `inline` element is a common early frustration with a one-word fix.

## Use logical properties

`margin-inline`, `padding-block`, `inset`. They adapt to writing direction, so a layout works in a right-to-left language without a separate stylesheet.

Slightly unfamiliar, no harder, and it removes a whole category of internationalisation work.

lessons.title: Flexbox and Grid: Choosing Between Them
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## One axis or two

**Flexbox** lays out along a single axis — a row or a column. Use it for a navigation bar, a toolbar, a card's internal stack, anything centred.

**Grid** lays out in two dimensions at once — rows and columns together. Use it for page layout and anything where items must align across both axes.

The instinct to reach for flexbox for everything produces nested flex containers faking a grid. When items need to align in both directions, use grid.

## Flexbox essentials

`display: flex` makes the children flex items. `justify-content` distributes along the main axis, `align-items` across it. `gap` spaces them without margins.

`flex: 1` makes an item take the remaining space. `flex-wrap: wrap` lets items move onto a new line rather than squashing.

## Grid essentials

`grid-template-columns` defines the tracks. `repeat(3, 1fr)` gives three equal columns; `1fr` means one share of the free space.

The pattern worth memorising:

```css
grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr));
```

That is a responsive grid with no media query at all. Columns are at least 250px, as many fit, and they share the leftover space. On a phone it becomes one column by itself.

## Centring, finally solved

`display: grid; place-items: center` centres a child horizontally and vertically in two lines. This used to be a famously awkward problem.

## `gap` instead of margins

Both layouts support `gap`, which spaces children without adding margin to the outer edges. No more `:last-child { margin-right: 0 }`.

## Named grid areas for page layout

`grid-template-areas` lets you draw the layout in the stylesheet as text. It is unusually readable, and rearranging the page for a different screen size is a matter of rewriting the picture.
keyTakeaways: Flexbox for one axis, grid for two — nested flex faking a grid is the smell
`gap` spaces children without edge margins in both systems
`repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr))` is a responsive grid with no media query
`display: grid; place-items: center` centres in two lines
`grid-template-areas` draws the page layout as readable text

lessons.title: Responsive Design, Mobile First
lessons.contentMarkdown: ## Start narrow Write the phone layout as the base, then add complexity at wider breakpoints with `min-width` queries. The alternative — designing wide and stripping down — means the mobile experience is a series of overrides and always feels like an afterthought. Most of your users are on a phone. Build for them first. ## The viewport meta tag is mandatory Without it, a phone renders your page at desktop width and scales it down, making everything unreadable. It is one line and every responsive page needs it. ## Breakpoints come from the content Do not copy a list of device widths; devices change every year. Widen the browser until the layout looks wrong, and put a breakpoint there. Use `rem` rather than `px` so breakpoints respect the user's font size setting. ## Prefer intrinsic sizing to breakpoints `minmax()`, `clamp()`, `auto-fit` and `flex-wrap` adapt continuously. Layouts built from them need far fewer media queries and behave sensibly at sizes you never tested. `clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 1.5rem)` scales type smoothly between a floor and a ceiling. ## Never cause horizontal scrolling The commonest mobile bug. Usually an element with a fixed width wider than the screen, a long unbroken string, or an image without `max-width: 100%`. Test at 375px. If the page scrolls sideways, it is broken. ## Images need sizing attributes Set `width` and `height` on every ``. The browser reserves the space before the image loads, preventing the content jumping as images arrive — which is both annoying and a measured ranking factor. `loading="lazy"` on below-the-fold images defers them. ## Respect user preferences `prefers-reduced-motion` for people who find animation uncomfortable or nauseating. `prefers-color-scheme` for dark mode. Both are two lines and ignoring them makes your site unusable for some people.
keyTakeaways: Write the narrow layout first and add at `min-width` breakpoints
The viewport meta tag is required or a phone renders at desktop width
Choose breakpoints where the content breaks, in rem, not from a device list
Intrinsic sizing with clamp and auto-fit needs far fewer media queries
Test at 375px for horizontal scroll; size images to prevent layout shift

lessons.title: Accessibility: Keyboard, Contrast and Screen Readers
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## It is part of the build

Accessibility retrofitted after an audit is expensive and half-done. Built in from the start it costs very little, because most of it is using the right element and not removing things the browser gives you.

It is also a legal requirement in many jurisdictions for public-facing services.

## Everything must work from the keyboard

Tab through your page. Every interactive element should be reachable, in a sensible order, with a visible focus indicator.

Never write `outline: none` without providing a replacement. Removing the focus ring because it is "ugly" makes the page unusable for anyone not using a mouse, and it is the single most common accessibility failure on the web.

Use `:focus-visible` to style focus for keyboard users without showing a ring on mouse clicks.

## Contrast is measurable

WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and interactive boundaries. Browser dev tools report the ratio directly, so this is checkable in seconds rather than a matter of opinion.

Light grey placeholder text almost always fails.

## Never rely on colour alone

A red border says nothing to a colour-blind user or a screen reader. Pair colour with text, an icon or a pattern.

The test: print it in greyscale. Is the meaning still there?

## ARIA is a last resort

The first rule of ARIA is not to use it. A `<button>` needs no `role="button"`. Incorrect ARIA is worse than none, because it overrides what the browser would have conveyed correctly.

Where it earns its place: `aria-label` for an icon-only button, `aria-live` for content updating without a page change, `aria-expanded` on a disclosure control.

## Announce dynamic changes

Content inserted by JavaScript is invisible to a screen reader unless it is in a live region. A search that updates results silently gives a screen reader user no indication anything happened.

## Test with real tools

Run axe or Lighthouse for the automated checks — they catch perhaps a third of issues. Then tab through the page, and try a screen reader for ten minutes. That ten minutes teaches more than any checklist.
keyTakeaways: Build it in from the start; retrofitting after an audit is expensive and partial
Never remove the focus outline without a replacement — use `:focus-visible`
Contrast is measurable: 4.5:1 for body text, checkable in dev tools
Never signal meaning by colour alone; test it in greyscale
Prefer native elements over ARIA, and announce dynamic updates in a live region

lessons.title: Values, Types and the Comparisons That Surprise You
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Seven primitives and objects

`string`, `number`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`, `symbol`, `bigint` are primitives. Everything else — arrays, functions, dates — is an object.

`typeof null` returns `"object"`. That is a bug from 1995 that can never be fixed without breaking the web.

## `==` coerces, `===` does not

`==` converts types before comparing, which produces results nobody wants: `0 == ""` is true, `null == undefined` is true, `"1" == 1` is true.

Use `===` always. The single exception worth knowing is `x == null`, which is a concise check for "null or undefined" — and even that is clearer written out.

## `null` versus `undefined`

`undefined` means a value was never set. `null` means it was deliberately set to nothing.

The distinction is real but easy to over-think. Be consistent: use `null` for intentional absence in your own code, and expect `undefined` from missing properties and parameters.

## Numbers are floating point

There is one number type, and `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` is false, exactly as in other languages.

For money, work in minor units as integers or use a decimal library. `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` is about 9 quadrillion — beyond that, use `BigInt`.

## Falsy values

`false`, `0`, `-0`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`. Everything else is truthy, including `"0"`, `"false"`, `[]` and `{}`.

`if (count)` is wrong when `0` is a legitimate value, which it usually is.

## Nullish operators for that exact problem

`??` falls back only on `null` or `undefined`, not on `0` or `""`. `||` falls back on any falsy value, which silently replaces a legitimate zero.

`?.` short-circuits on null or undefined instead of throwing, which removes a lot of defensive nesting.

## Prefer `const`

`const` by default, `let` when reassignment is genuinely needed, never `var`. `var` is function-scoped and hoisted, which produces bugs that block scoping does not.
keyTakeaways: `typeof null` is `"object"` — a permanent historical bug
Use `===`; `==` coerces and produces results nobody intends

`0`, `""` and `NaN` are falsy — `if (count)` is wrong when zero is valid
`??` falls back only on null or undefined, unlike `||`

lessons.title: Functions, Closures and `this`
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Functions are values

You can pass a function as an argument, return one, and store one in an object. This is why callbacks, array methods and event handlers all work the way they do.

## Closures capture the surrounding scope

A function defined inside another can read the outer function's variables — and keeps access to them after the outer function has returned.

This is how you make private state, memoise a result, and write a counter without a global. It is also how you accidentally hold a large object in memory: a closure keeps everything it references alive.

## Arrow functions differ in `this`

An arrow function has no `this` of its own; it uses the one from where it was defined. A regular function's `this` depends on how it is *called*.

That difference is the entire reason arrow functions solved the "`this` is undefined in my callback" problem that dominated older JavaScript.

## What `this` refers to

- Called as a method — the object before the dot.
- Called standalone — `undefined` in strict mode and in modules.
- With `call`, `apply` or `bind` — whatever you passed.
- In an arrow function — the enclosing scope's `this`.

Passing a method as a callback detaches it from its object, which is the classic source of `this` being wrong. An arrow function or `bind` fixes it.

## Prefer the array methods

`map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `find`, `some` and `every` say what you mean. `forEach` when you genuinely want a side effect.

Note which mutate: `sort`, `reverse` and `splice` change the array in place. `toSorted` and `toReversed` return a copy, which is usually what you wanted.

## Destructuring and spread

`const { name, email } = user` and `{ ...defaults, ...overrides }` are idiomatic and read clearly. Note that spread is a shallow copy — nested objects are still shared.

## Default parameters are evaluated per call

Unlike Python, JavaScript evaluates a default expression on every call that omits the argument. `function f(items = [])` is safe here.
keyTakeaways: Functions are values; closures keep access to the scope they were defined in
A closure keeps everything it references alive — a real source of leaks
An arrow function inherits `this`; a regular function's depends on the call
Passing a method as a callback detaches `this` — bind it or use an arrow
`sort` and `reverse` mutate; `toSorted` and `toReversed` return copies

modules.summary: The DOM, events, and the single thread everything shares.

lessons.title: The DOM and Events
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The DOM is a live tree

The browser parses your HTML into a tree of nodes. JavaScript can read and change it, and the page updates immediately.

`querySelector` and `querySelectorAll` find elements with CSS selector syntax. `querySelectorAll` returns a static NodeList — it does not update as the document changes, which is usually what you want.

## Prefer `textContent`

`innerHTML` parses its input as HTML. Assigning user-supplied content to it is a cross-site scripting vulnerability: a string containing a script-bearing tag executes.

`textContent` sets text without parsing. Use it unless you genuinely need to insert markup, and in that case sanitise first.

## Events bubble

A click on a button fires on the button, then its parent, then upward to the document. That is why a single listener on a container can handle clicks on all its children.

This *delegation* is not just tidier — it works for elements added later, and it is one listener instead of a hundred.

## Batch DOM changes

Every read of a layout property (`offsetHeight`, `getBoundingClientRect`) forces the browser to recalculate layout if anything changed since the last one. Alternating reads and writes in a loop — layout thrashing — is a classic performance disaster.

Read everything, then write everything. Build a fragment off-document and insert it once rather than appending in a loop.

## Remove listeners you added

A listener on a removed element keeps that element and everything its handler closes over alive. `AbortController` removes a whole group of listeners in one call, which is much harder to get wrong.

## `preventDefault` and `stopPropagation` are different

`preventDefault` stops the browser's default behaviour — following a link, submitting a form. `stopPropagation` stops the event travelling to ancestors.

Reaching for `stopPropagation` to fix an interaction problem usually hides a design problem, and it breaks delegation elsewhere.
keyTakeaways: `querySelectorAll` returns a static list; the DOM tree itself is live
`innerHTML` with user content is an XSS vulnerability — use `textContent`
Events bubble, so one delegated listener handles children including future ones
Interleaving layout reads and writes causes thrashing — read then write
`AbortController` removes a group of listeners in one call

lessons.title: The Event Loop: Why the Page Freezes
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## One thread does everything

JavaScript, layout, painting and event handling all share one thread per tab. While your code runs, nothing else can — no clicks are processed, no animation advances, nothing repaints.

That is why a long synchronous loop freezes the page completely. It is not slow; it is blocked.

## How the loop works

Synchronous code runs to completion. Then the loop takes the next task from the queue and runs that to completion. Repeat.

Asynchronous operations — timers, network requests, events — do not run your callback immediately. They queue it, and it runs when the current work finishes.

## Microtasks jump the queue

Promise callbacks go in the *microtask* queue, which is fully drained after the current task and before the next macrotask (a timer, an event).

This is why a resolved promise's `.then` runs before a `setTimeout(..., 0)` queued earlier. Worth knowing when ordering surprises you.

## `setTimeout(fn, 0)` is not immediate

It means "as soon as the current work and all pending microtasks are done". The real delay can be far more than zero, and browsers clamp nested timers.

Its legitimate use is yielding: letting the browser paint before continuing.

## Long work must be broken up or moved

For a long computation, either chunk it and yield between chunks, or move it to a **Web Worker**, which runs on its own thread and communicates by messages.

A worker cannot touch the DOM, which is the point — the DOM is not thread-safe.

## Throttle and debounce high-frequency events

Scroll and resize fire continuously. **Debounce** waits until the activity stops — right for a search box. **Throttle** limits to once per interval — right for scroll position.

For anything visual, `requestAnimationFrame` schedules the work just before the next paint, which is exactly the right moment.

lessons.title: Promises, async/await and fetch
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## A promise is a future value

Pending, then either fulfilled or rejected. `await` suspends the function until it settles, without blocking the thread — other work proceeds.

## `fetch` does not reject on HTTP errors

This is the trap. A 404 or a 500 **fulfils** the promise. Only a network failure rejects it.

So `await fetch(url)` followed by `response.json()` on a 500 tries to parse an error page as JSON and produces a confusing error a long way from the cause.

Always check `response.ok` first.

## Always set a timeout

`fetch` has no default timeout. A server that accepts the connection and never responds leaves a spinner turning forever.

`AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` handles this in one argument, and the same signal lets you cancel when the user navigates away.

## Run independent requests in parallel

Two sequential awaits take the sum of their durations. `Promise.all` starts both and takes the longer.

`Promise.all` rejects as soon as any one fails. `Promise.allSettled` waits for all and reports each outcome, which is what you want when partial results are useful.

## Handle the error, do not just log it

A `catch` that only calls `console.error` leaves the user staring at a spinner. Every failure needs a user-visible outcome.

## Avoid the race condition

A user types quickly and you fire three searches. They can return out of order, and the response to "ab" can arrive after the one for "abc", leaving the wrong results on screen.

Abort the previous request, or tag each one and ignore stale responses.

## Do not mix `.then` and `await`

Pick one. Mixed code is harder to follow and makes error handling inconsistent. `async`/`await` with `try`/`catch` reads best in most cases.
keyTakeaways: `await` suspends the function without blocking the thread
`fetch` does not reject on 404 or 500 — always check `response.ok`
Set a timeout with `AbortSignal.timeout`; fetch has no default
`Promise.all` for independent requests; `allSettled` when partial results help
Abort or tag requests, or a slow earlier response overwrites a newer one

lessons.title: Handling Every State: Loading, Empty, Error, Data
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Four states, not one

Every piece of fetched data can be in four states, and users will encounter all of them:

1. **Loading** — the request is in flight.
2. **Empty** — it succeeded and there is nothing to show.
3. **Error** — it failed.
4. **Data** — it succeeded with results.

Most beginner code handles the fourth and leaves the other three as a blank screen. A blank screen is indistinguishable from a broken page.

## Empty is not an error

"No results for 'xyzzy'" and "Could not reach the server" are completely different situations and must look different. Conflating them teaches users to distrust the interface.

An empty state is also an opportunity: suggest what to try, or offer the action that creates the first item.

## Error messages should say what to do

"Error: 500" tells a user nothing. "We could not load your orders. Try again in a moment." tells them it is not their fault and that retrying is reasonable.

Include a retry button. Most failures are transient, and a button is far better than asking someone to reload the page and lose their place.

## Model the state explicitly

A discriminated union — one object with a `status` field — makes it impossible to be loading and errored at once. Separate `isLoading` and `error` booleans allow four combinations, two of which are nonsense.

This also makes the rendering a single switch, so forgetting a case is visible.

## Announce changes to screen readers

Swapping content in without a page change is silent to assistive technology. An `aria-live` region announces "Loading" and "14 results found".

## Do not flash the spinner

For a request that takes 80ms, a spinner appearing and vanishing is worse than nothing. Delay showing it by 200-300ms; most requests finish first.

## Keep the previous data during a refresh

When reloading existing data, showing the old data dimmed is better than replacing everything with a spinner. The user keeps their context.

lessons.title: Types That Describe Your Data
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## It is JavaScript with the shapes written down

TypeScript compiles to JavaScript and adds no runtime behaviour. Everything it does happens while you type and when you build.

The payoff is real: a typo in a property name, a function called with the wrong arguments, a field that might be undefined — all caught before the code runs.

## Infer where obvious, annotate at boundaries

`const count = 0` is inferred as `number`. Writing `: number` there adds noise.

Annotate where it matters: function parameters, return types on exported functions, and anything crossing a boundary. Those are the places a wrong assumption travels furthest.

## Model your domain

An `interface` or `type` for your data is documentation the compiler enforces. `Order` says exactly what an order has, and misspelling `custmerId` fails to compile rather than producing `undefined` at runtime.

## Unions express "one of these"

`type Status = "draft" | "paid" | "cancelled"` is far better than `string`. A typo is a compile error, your editor autocompletes the options, and a `switch` can be checked for exhaustiveness.

## Optional versus undefined

`email?: string` means the property may be absent. `email: string | undefined` means it must be present and may hold undefined. The distinction matters when constructing objects.

## `unknown`, never `any`

`any` switches off checking for that value and everything derived from it, and it spreads silently through a codebase.

`unknown` is the safe version: you may hold it, but you must narrow it before use. For data arriving from outside — an API response, JSON from storage — `unknown` plus a validation step is the correct pattern.

## Turn on `strict`

`strict: true` enables the checks that make TypeScript worth using, particularly `strictNullChecks`. Without it, every type silently includes null and undefined, and the tool catches far less.

Start strict on a new project.
keyTakeaways: TypeScript adds no runtime behaviour — it checks while you write and build
Let inference handle the obvious; annotate boundaries and exported signatures
String literal unions beat `string` for fixed sets of values

lessons.title: Narrowing, Unions and Avoiding the Cast
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## A cast is a promise, not a check

`value as Order` tells the compiler to stop asking questions. Nothing is verified. If you are wrong, the error surfaces somewhere else entirely, and the type annotation actively misleads the next reader.

Narrowing is the alternative: prove the type with a check the compiler understands.

## The compiler follows your checks

`typeof x === "string"`, `Array.isArray(x)`, `x instanceof Error`, `"kind" in x`, and a plain `if (x)` all narrow the type inside the branch. You do not need to cast afterwards.

## Discriminated unions

Give each variant a shared literal field and the compiler can tell them apart:

```ts
type Result =
  | { status: "ok"; data: Order }
  | { status: "error"; message: string };
```

Inside `if (result.status === "ok")`, `result.data` is available and `result.message` is not. That is the whole pattern, and it models almost every "one of these outcomes" situation.

## Exhaustiveness checking

Assign the narrowed value to `never` in the default branch. When someone adds a variant, every switch missing it fails to compile — pointing you at each place that must handle it.

This turns a whole class of runtime bug into a build error.

## Type predicates for reusable checks

A function returning `value is Order` performs a real runtime check and narrows the type for the caller. Unlike a cast, it verifies.

## Prefer `satisfies` to an annotation for config objects

`satisfies` checks that a value conforms to a type while keeping its specific inferred type. You get validation without losing the literal types.

## Zod or Valibot at the boundary

Hand-written type guards get tedious. A schema library validates at runtime and derives the TypeScript type from the same schema, so the two cannot drift apart.
keyTakeaways: A cast asserts without checking; narrowing proves it to the compiler
`typeof`, `instanceof`, `in` and truthiness all narrow inside the branch
A discriminated union plus a switch models any set of outcomes
Assign to `never` in the default branch for exhaustiveness checking
Use a schema library at the boundary so the type and the check cannot drift

modules.title: Tooling
modules.summary: What npm and a bundler actually do, and what a framework adds on top.

lessons.title: npm, Modules and a Build You Understand
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## npm installs, and records what it installed

`package.json` lists your direct dependencies. `package-lock.json` records the exact resolved versions of everything, including transitive dependencies.

Commit the lock file. Without it, your colleague and your CI server get different versions and "works on my machine" becomes a real conversation.

Use `npm ci` in CI: it installs exactly the lock file, and fails if the two disagree.

## Version ranges

`^1.2.3` accepts any 1.x. `~1.2.3` accepts 1.2.x. `1.2.3` accepts only that.

The caret is the default and usually fine, because the lock file pins the actual version. The range only matters when the lock is regenerated.

## dependencies versus devDependencies

Anything the shipped code imports is a dependency. Build tools, test runners and type definitions are devDependencies and never reach production.

## ES modules

`import` and `export` are the standard. They are statically analysable, which is what lets a bundler remove code you do not use.

Prefer named exports. A default export can be imported under any name, so the same module gets three different names across a codebase.

## What a bundler does

Vite, esbuild or Rollup follow your imports, produce a dependency graph, and emit a small number of optimised files.

Concretely: it resolves bare imports the browser cannot, transpiles TypeScript and modern syntax, removes unused exports, minifies, adds content hashes to filenames for caching, and splits code so a route's JavaScript loads only when that route does.

## Know what is in your bundle

Run a bundle analyser occasionally. A 300KB date library imported for one function, or a whole icon set pulled in for three icons, is common and usually a one-line fix.

## Keep the dependency count honest

Every dependency is code you ship, a supply-chain risk and a future upgrade. For anything you could write in twenty lines, write the twenty lines.
keyTakeaways: Commit the lock file and use `npm ci`; without it environments diverge
devDependencies never reach production — keep build and test tools there
Named exports over default; a default can be renamed by every importer
A bundler resolves, transpiles, tree-shakes, minifies, hashes and splits
Check the bundle occasionally; every dependency is shipped code and future work

lessons.title: From Vanilla to a Framework: What Angular Adds
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Why frameworks exist

Hand-written DOM manipulation works, and stops scaling at a predictable point. Once several parts of a page depend on the same state, keeping the DOM in agreement with that state by hand becomes the bulk of the work — and the bulk of the bugs.

A framework's core contribution is this: you describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and it handles making the DOM match.

## What Angular provides

- **Components** — a template, styles and logic packaged with a defined input and output contract.
- **Data binding** — the template re-renders when the data changes; you never write `element.textContent = ...`.
- **Dependency injection** — the same idea as on the server, and the same benefit for testing.
- **Routing** — URL to component, with lazy loading per route.
- **Forms** — validation, state and error display as a system rather than ad hoc.
- **HTTP client** — typed requests with interceptors for auth and errors.
- **TypeScript throughout** — Angular assumes it, which is why the earlier TypeScript work matters.

## The cost is real

A framework is more to learn, more to ship, and a set of conventions you must follow. For a landing page or a small widget it is overhead with no return.

The honest boundary: a handful of interactive elements, use the platform. An application with routing, shared state and many screens, use a framework.

## The concepts transfer

Components, one-way data flow, lifecycle, dependency injection and reactive state appear in React, Vue and Svelte too, under different names.

Learning one well means learning the second in days. That is why the fundamentals in this path matter more than the framework choice.

## Your platform knowledge does not become obsolete

Every framework renders to the DOM, is subject to the event loop, and inherits the box model. Framework users who do not know the platform get stuck the moment something behaves unexpectedly — and they cannot debug it, because the abstraction is where they stopped looking.
keyTakeaways: Frameworks exist so you describe the UI for a state, not the steps to update it
Angular brings components, binding, DI, routing, forms and a typed HTTP client
For a few interactive elements the platform is enough; an app needs a framework
Components, one-way flow and lifecycle transfer across all the major frameworks
Platform knowledge is what lets you debug when the abstraction behaves oddly

modules.summary: Performance measured on a real device, and tests that check behaviour.

lessons.title: Performance on a Real Device
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Your laptop is not the test

You are on a fast machine with a fast connection and a warm cache. Your users are frequently on a mid-range phone on mobile data.

Throttle the CPU to 4x slowdown and the network to Slow 4G in dev tools. That is a far more honest picture, and it is usually uncomfortable the first time.

## Measure the metrics users feel

- **Largest Contentful Paint** — when the main content appears. Target under 2.5s.
- **Interaction to Next Paint** — how quickly the page responds to input. Target under 200ms.
- **Cumulative Layout Shift** — how much content jumps as it loads. Target under 0.1.

These correspond to what people actually experience: is it there, does it respond, does it stay still.

## JavaScript is the usual culprit

A large bundle must be downloaded, parsed and executed before anything is interactive, and parsing is where a slow device really suffers.

The fixes, in order of impact: split by route, defer what is not needed immediately, and remove dependencies you barely use.

## Images are the other one

Serve modern formats. Size them for the space they occupy — a 3000px image in a 400px slot wastes most of the bytes. Set `width` and `height` so the space is reserved, and `loading="lazy"` below the fold.

## Layout shift has a small number of causes

Images without dimensions, web fonts swapping, and content injected above existing content. Each has a standard fix: size attributes, `font-display: optional` or a matched fallback metric, and reserving space for anything that will arrive.

## Cache deliberately

Content-hashed filenames can be cached for a year, because a change produces a new name. The HTML must not be, or nobody gets the new version.

## Measure, change one thing, measure again

Run Lighthouse before and after. Performance work done by intuition frequently makes things worse, and without a before-and-after you will not know.

lessons.title: Testing Front-End Code
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Test what a user does

The most useful front-end tests interact the way a person does: find the button by its visible label, click it, and check what appears.

Tests written against CSS classes and DOM structure break every time the markup is tidied, teaching the team that failures are noise.

## Query the way people perceive

Testing Library's guidance is to find elements by role and accessible name — `getByRole("button", { name: "Create account" })`.

This has a useful side effect: if your test cannot find the element that way, a screen reader user probably cannot either. The test surfaces accessibility problems for free.

## Three levels

- **Unit** — pure functions: formatting, validation, calculation. Fast, and where most cases belong.
- **Component** — render a component, interact, assert. Vitest with Testing Library.
- **End-to-end** — a real browser over a real flow with Playwright. Slow, so keep them few and important.

Most tests should be the first two.

## Do not test the framework

`@if` works. Your template's conditional rendering does not need a test proving the framework functions.

Test your logic, your states and your edge cases.

## Cover all four states

Loading, empty, error and data. The error and empty cases are the ones nobody clicks through manually, and therefore the ones that break.

## Mock at the network boundary

Intercept HTTP rather than stubbing your own service classes. Then your real data-fetching code runs, including the error handling, and the test survives refactoring.

## One end-to-end test of the critical path

Sign in, do the main thing, sign out — in a real browser. This catches the build-level failures no unit test can: a missing asset, a broken route, a content security policy blocking a script.
keyTakeaways: Test by visible label and role, the way a user perceives the page
Queries that fail by accessible name often reveal a real accessibility problem
Mostly unit and component tests; keep end-to-end tests few
